passages.happening:
David summons all the leaders of Israel to Jerusalem: the tribal leaders, the commanders, the stewards, the court officials and the mighty men (verse 1). He rises and says, “Listen to me, my brothers and my people. It was in my heart to build a house as a resting place for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and as a footstool for our God” (verse 2). But God said that he was a man of war who had spilled blood (verse 3). God chose Judah, then David's family, then David, and of all David's sons ‘He has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel’ (verse 5). God has promised to establish Solomon's kingdom forever, ‘if he resolutely carries out My commandments and ordinances, as is being done this day’ (verse 7).

David charges the assembly to ‘keep and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God’ (verse 8). Then to Solomon: “know the God of your father and serve Him wholeheartedly and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches every heart and understands the intent of every thought. If you seek Him, He will be found by you; but if you forsake Him, He will reject you forever” (verse 9). “Be strong and do it” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
After the long lists, the story resumes with a public ceremony. The officials just organized are called together, and David, old and near the end, speaks to them as a father and a king. The scene belongs to the last years of his reign, around 970 BC.

First Kings 1 tells the succession very differently, as a tense struggle in the palace: David's older son Adonijah tried to take the throne, and Nathan and Bathsheba moved David to name Solomon. Chronicles leaves that out and shows a calm, public commissioning. The two accounts need not conflict. The Chronicler knew his readers had Kings, and he chose the side of the succession that concerned the temple and the nation's covenant with God.

The ark was imagined as the footstool, hadom, of the invisible God enthroned above the cherubim. The temple would not contain God; it would be where his feet, as it were, touched the earth. The kingdom is called the kingdom of the LORD: Solomon will sit on God's throne, not merely his father's. In chapter 17 the promise was given without a condition; here it comes with one for Solomon himself, if he keeps God's commands (verse 7). Seek, darash, is the measure Chronicles uses for every king; its opposite, azav, to forsake, frames both the warning in verse 9 and the comfort in verse 20.
passages.later: Isaiah heard God say, “Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me?” (Isaiah 66:1). Jeremiah wrote to the exiles, ‘You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart’ (Jeremiah 29:13).
passages.asks: David told his son that the LORD searches every heart and is found by those who seek him. Ask what God sees when he searches yours. And ask whether you serve him with a willing mind or only out of duty.

passages.t: The plan, given in writing, and be strong
passages.happening:
David gives Solomon the plans for the temple, its buildings, storerooms and inner rooms, and the room for the mercy seat (verse 11), for the courts, the treasuries, the divisions of priests and Levites and all the work of service (verses 12-13). He sets out the weight of gold and silver for every lampstand, table, bowl and dish, the gold for the altar of incense, and ‘the plans for the chariot of the gold cherubim that spread their wings and overshadowed the ark of the covenant of the LORD’ (verse 18). “All this,” he says, “the LORD has made clear to me in writing by His hand upon me” (verse 19).

David says to Solomon, “Be strong and courageous, and do it. Do not be afraid or discouraged, for the LORD God, my God, is with you. He will neither fail you nor forsake you before all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished” (verse 20). The priests, the Levites, every willing craftsman, the officials and all the people are ready (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The word for the plan, tavnit, is the word used when God showed Moses the pattern of the tabernacle on the mountain. Using it here places David beside Moses as the one through whom God gave the design for Israel's worship. Metals were valued by weight, not coin, and the word weight comes again and again. The lampstands, the tables for the bread of the Presence and the incense altar echo the tabernacle's furnishings in Exodus. The chariot of the cherubim pictures the ark and its cherubim as God's throne-chariot, an image Ezekiel later saw in motion.

The closing words echo Moses' charge to Joshua: be strong and courageous, do not be afraid, God will not forsake you. The Chronicler frames the handover from David to Solomon like the one from Moses to Joshua, from a leader who could not finish to one who would.

For the Chronicler's first readers, worshiping in a rebuilt temple that was modest beside Solomon's, this mattered. Their worship came from a plan God had given and an order David had set. They were not inventing religion; they were continuing what God had given.
passages.later: God told Moses, ‘You must make the tabernacle and design all its furnishings according to the pattern I show you’ (Exodus 25:9). A psalm says, ‘Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool’ (Psalm 132:7).
passages.asks: David could hand Solomon the plan, the gold and the people, but not the courage. Ask what you have been given to finish that you are afraid to begin. And ask whether you believe God will not forsake you before the work is done.
